newsitem.title: TAIWAN: Taiwan shows off "unequal treaties" that ceded HK.
newsitem.headline: Taiwan shows off "unequal treaties" that ceded HK.

text.p: When Britain's Prince Charles hands Hong Kong over to Chinese President Jiang Zemin on Monday, the ceremony will not feature a ritual ripping up of the newly obsolete Treaty of Nanking.
It can't. The yellowing "unequal treaty" won't be there.

China's copy of the infamous 1842 document by which Britain forced the Qing dynasty emperor Daoguang to cede Hong Kong to Queen Victoria remains under guard in Taipei -- the seat since 1949 of the exiled Republic of China.
Keen to exploit the media spotlight generated by Hong Kong's handover, Taipei is putting all four treaties related to Hong Kong's cession on public display from Saturday.

Foreign Minister John Chang said the exhibition aimed to remind Beijing and the world of the Nationalist republic's continuing, if constrained, existence on the eve of Hong Kong's absorption by communist China.
"The United Kingdom did not come to us to negotiate the return of Hong Kong, but the Republic of China does exist," Chang told Reuters in an interview.

"Actually, in our view it (Hong Kong) should be returned to China, to the side which still holds the lease and the treaty -- which are in our possession," he said. "We hope to help people understand the truth about a part of history."
Beijing has regarded Taiwan as a rebel-held province since the Nationalists fled there after losing the civil war on the mainland. The sides have no official contacts.

Palace Museum director Chin Hsiao-yi said Beijing deserved little credit for ending western colonialism in Asia,as it was the Nationalists who toppled the Qing and undermined the unequal treaties long before the 1949 communist takeover.
"The return of Hong Kong is our victory," Chin said as he displayed the treaties, each hand-lettered in Chinese and English, bound in silk and bearing wax seals and imprints.

Chin said the display of the treaties of Nanking, Tianjin and Beijing governing Hong Kong's cession, and the 99-year lease of 1898 that gave Britain additional land adjoining the colony carried modern lessons for Hong Kong, Taiwan and communist China.
"The importance of the exhibition is to raise awareness of freedom and democracy in the three places," he said.
"Hong Kong has enjoyed great freedoms in these 20 years but not democracy. Its return to the Chinese nation worries us as to whether it can retain its freedoms and develop democracy."
Foreign Ministry archivist Jeffrey Liu said the treaties under his care have grave importance for Chinese everywhere -- whether in Hong Kong, Taiwan or the communist-ruled mainland.
"The Treaty of Nanking was the first unequal treaty signed between the Qing dynasty and foreign powers, enabling them to seize power and invade the country," Liu told Reuters.
"This is the shame of the Chinese nation. The treaty is a reminder of this shame for Chinese wherever they are."
The Treaty of Nanking was signed in what today is the Yangtse river port of Nanjing, which in 1842 was the farthest inland penetration of British "gunboat diplomacy".
Four copies still exist, two working drafts and two final versions approved personally by the emperor and queen.
Of the latter, one resides in Britain and another deep in the bowels of Taipei's Foreign Ministry archives, inside a heavy safe in a temperature- and humidity-controlled vault.
After the Qing dynasty collapsed in 1911, the Qing archives passed to the new Republic of China.

Japan's 1927 invasion and China's 1940s civil war forced republican archivists to move the documents several times. Only the most important treaties were taken when the defeated Nationalists fled into exile on Taiwan.
